inline.s: [Śāriputra, I now clearly tell you: as a good spiritual friend, with a compassionate mind, one seeks benefit, joy, and security for others
(the same as “secure”)
; you should single-mindedly listen to and receive my words, always seeking the good benefit, and never be indolent.]

Śāriputra, I now clearly tell you that one should act as a good spiritual friend, and with a compassionate heart seek benefit, joy, and security for others. You should single-mindedly listen to and receive my words, always seeking the good benefit and never letting the mind be indolent.

[Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma has five faults. What are the five? First, he claims himself to have fully known the Buddha Dharma; second, when preaching the Buddhist scriptures, he brings up the fault that the scriptures contradict one another; third, in his mind he doubts and does not believe the dharmas; fourth, with his own knowledge he condemns the Dharma of other scriptures; fifth, for the sake of profit and offerings he preaches the Dharma for others. Śāriputra, I say that such a person will fall into hell and will not reach nirvāṇa.]

Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma has five faults. What are the five? First, he claims himself to have fully known the Buddha Dharma; second, when preaching the Buddhist scriptures, he points out the fault that the scriptures contradict one another (the Buddha preaches the Dharma through the two truths — the conventional and the ultimate; the impure preacher, knowing only how to grasp at appearances and not comprehending their meaning, actually declares the scriptures to be contradictory); third, in his mind he doubts and does not believe the dharmas; fourth, with his own knowledge he rashly criticizes the teachings as erroneous; fifth, for the sake of profit and offerings he preaches the Dharma for others. Śāriputra, I say that such a person will fall into hell and will not reach nirvāṇa.

[Two truths] The conventional truth and the ultimate truth. The conventional truth is also called the worldly truth or the truth of mundane convention — that is, the worldly phenomena seen by ordinary beings. The ultimate truth is also called the foremost meaning truth, or the supreme meaning truth — that is, the real principle seen by the wisdom of the sages, namely the inexpressible Dharma-nature realized inwardly. The Great Perfection of Wisdom Treatise says: “In the Buddha Dharma there are two truths: first, the worldly truth; second, the foremost meaning truth. For the sake of the worldly truth, it is said that there are sentient beings; for the sake of the foremost meaning truth, it is said that sentient beings have no existence.”

[Moreover, Śāriputra, when a preaching bhikṣu is present in the great assembly, and those who believe and delight in the Dharma spread a high seat for him, he abandons the Buddha’s right Dharma and preaches the finely adorned words of the outsiders. This Dharma-treasure, which I for a long time sought with diligent effort and hardship, this evil person sets aside and does not preach. Rather, with the contradictory meanings in the scriptures, he mutually affirms and denies, not following the right Dharma; in the Dharma of the sages he is lofty and arrogant, preaching at will for the sake of profit and offerings.]

Moreover, Śāriputra, when a preaching bhikṣu is present in the great assembly, and those who believe and delight in the Buddha Dharma spread a high seat for him, he abandons the Buddha’s right Dharma and preaches the fallacious theories that the outsiders adorn with fine words. This Dharma-treasure, which I through long eons sought with diligent effort and hardship, this evil person sets aside and does not preach. Rather, taking the contradictory meanings in the scriptures, he censures them, not following the right Dharma; in the Dharma of the sages he is arrogant and self-important, preaching at will for the sake of profit and offerings.

[Adorned with fine words] The wrong doctrines of the outsiders dare not state their principle plainly, clearly, and directly; instead, sparing no effort and going round about, they dress it up in gorgeous, flowery language — what the common saying calls “winding round and round” — in order to attain a hidden intent that cannot be spoken of.

[Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma mixed with the meaning of the outsiders, any good bhikṣu who diligently seeks the path should rise from his seat and go. Why? Śāriputra, because a believing layman has spread a high seat for him, he ought not to preach the meaning of the outsiders; if he does not leave, he is not a good bhikṣu, nor is he called one who follows the Buddha’s teaching.]

Śāriputra, this bhikṣu preaches the Dharma mixed with the meaning of the outsiders; if in the assembly there is a good bhikṣu who diligently seeks the path, he should leave. Why? Śāriputra, because a believing layman has spread a high seat for the preacher, the preacher ought not to preach the meaning of the outsiders. Now he, in pursuit of fame and profit, caters to the believers and preaches at will; if the diligent seeker does not leave, he is not a good bhikṣu, nor is he one who follows the Buddha’s teaching.

[Śāriputra, it is very difficult to preach the Dharma. One who preaches thus, I say, is called an outsider, a disciple of the Nirgranthas, not a disciple of the Buddha. After this preacher’s life ends, he will be born in the path of the Nirgranthas. What is the path of the Nirgranthas? Wrong views are the path of the Nirgranthas. What are wrong views? They are the hell realm, the animal realm, and the hungry ghost realm.]

Śāriputra, it is very difficult to preach the right Dharma. One who preaches so at will, I say, is a disciple of the Nirgrantha outsiders and not a disciple of the Buddha. After this preacher’s life ends, he will be born in the path of the Nirgranthas. What is the path of the Nirgranthas? The path of wrong views is the path of the Nirgranthas. What is the path of wrong views? It is the hell realm, the animal realm, and the hungry ghost realm.
[Nirgrantha (niqianzi)] One of the six great outsiders; it is also commonly used as a general name for those who leave home among the outsiders.

[Why? Śāriputra, one who has not personally realized the Dharma yet sits on the high seat, who himself does not know yet teaches others, will certainly fall into hell. Śāriputra, such causes and conditions the Tathāgata fully knows. My disciples, through various gates, various causes and conditions, and various views, destroy my right Dharma. Śāriputra, if any sentient being hears this sutra — the foremost meaning emptiness, the Dharma of non-existence — and rejoices in mind, one should know that such a person is truly my disciple.]

Why? Śāriputra, one who has not personally realized the Dharma yet sits on the high seat and preaches the Dharma, who himself does not know the Dharma yet teaches the Dharma to others, will certainly fall into hell. Śāriputra, such causes and conditions the Tathāgata fully knows. My disciples, through various gates, various causes and conditions, and various views, destroy my right Dharma. Śāriputra, if any sentient being hears this sutra — the foremost meaning emptiness, the Dharma of non-existence — and rejoices in mind, one should know that such persons are truly my disciples.

[Foremost meaning emptiness] In the Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra the Buddha says: “All dharmas are false and illusory; the place where they cease is called the real, called the real mark, called the Dharma-realm, called ultimate wisdom, called the foremost meaning truth, called the foremost meaning emptiness.” [Foremost meaning truth] The supreme, perfect, and ultimate truth.

[Śāriputra, in a past age there were five hundred blind people walking along a road. They came to a great city, exhausted with hunger and thirst. They had one blind person remain outside to guard the goods, while the rest entered the city to beg for food and drink. Before long a deceiver came to the guard of the goods and said: “Hey! Why do you stay here alone?” He replied: “I have many companions who have entered the city to beg for food.” The deceiver said: “Do you not know? There is a great distribution of clothing, food, necklaces, flowers, incense, and various things that you can have as you wish. If you need them, I will take you there.” He replied: “Very well.” The deceiver then led the blind man a little way from his place and robbed him of all his goods.]

Śāriputra, in a past age there were five hundred blind people walking along a road. They came to a great city, exhausted with hunger and thirst, so they had one blind person remain outside the city to guard the luggage, while the rest entered the city to beg for food and drink. Before long a swindler came to the guard and said: “Hey! Why do you stay here alone?” The guard replied: “I have many companions; they have entered the city to beg for food.” The swindler said: “Do you not know? There they are making a great distribution of clothing, food, necklaces, flowers, incense, and various things that you can have as you wish. If you want to go, I will take you there.” The guard replied: “All right.” The swindler then led this blind man away from his place and robbed him of all his goods.

[The blind people begged for food and, having obtained it, returned. The deceiver again said to the blind people: “Did you encounter the giving of the great assembly?” They answered: “We did not.” The deceiver said: “You may place what you have obtained here; I will take you to the great assembly’s giving.” The blind people all left their goods together in one place and followed the deceiver. The deceiver brought all five hundred blind people to the edge of a great deep pit and said to them: “This ground is level and good, and there is a great assembly’s giving. You may each turn and walk east to receive others’ gifts.” Thereupon, all at once, they fell into the pit and died.]

The blind people who had entered the city to beg for food, having obtained it, returned. The swindler again said to them: “Did you encounter the giving of the great assembly?” They answered: “We did not.” The swindler said: “Place what you have obtained here; I will take you to the place of the great assembly’s giving.” The blind people all left their goods in one place and followed the swindler. The swindler brought these five hundred blind people to the edge of a great deep pit and said to them: “This ground is level and good, and here is the great assembly’s giving. Turn and walk east, and you will obtain the gifts that are given.” The blind people, acting as the swindler told them, all fell into the pit and died.

[Śāriputra, future bhikṣus will be fond of reading the outsiders’ scriptures; when they preach the Dharma they will embellish their words so as to make the assembly rejoice. At that time the evil Māra will assist them in deluding the multitude and obstructing the good Dharma. If there are those who greedily cling to sound, to speech, to cleverly adorned words, or even those who are fond of reading the outsiders’ scriptures, Māra will delude them all and make their minds secure and at ease. If there are bhikṣus who truly cultivate the Buddha Dharma, Māra causes the multitude to give rise to doubt toward them, so that they no longer make offerings to them. Or, if there are bhikṣus who have in some measure — two or three — already read the Buddha scriptures, Māra makes them seek the outsiders’ scriptures and teachings, praising them as good and excellent. These people, deluded by Māra, with the eye of wisdom covered and obstructed, deeply greedy for profit and offerings, read the various outside books, just like a flock of the blind deceived by a swindler, all made to fall into a deep pit and die.]

Śāriputra, future bhikṣus will be fond of reading the outsiders’ scriptures; when preaching the Dharma they will hide and adorn it with beautiful words, making the assembly rejoice. At that time the evil Māra assists him in deluding the multitude and obstructing the propagation of the good Dharma. If there are those who greedily cling to sound, to speech, and to cleverly adorned words, and who are also fond of reading the outsiders’ scriptures, Māra deludes them all and makes their minds secure and at ease. If there are bhikṣus who truly cultivate the Buddha Dharma, Māra causes the multitude to give rise to doubt toward them, so that they no longer make offerings to them. Or, if there are bhikṣus — two or three of them — who have already read the Buddha scriptures, Māra misleads them into seeking the outsiders’ scriptures and teachings, praising them as good and excellent. These people, deluded by Māra, with the eye of wisdom covered and obstructed, deeply greedy for profit and offerings, go to read the various outside books, just like a flock of the blind deceived by a swindler, falling into a deep pit and dying.

[Śāriputra, those born blind are the bhikṣus: they abandon the Buddha’s unsurpassed path and seek the outsiders’ scriptures. The swindler is the evil Māra; the deep pit is the wrong path. Śāriputra, just as the flock of the blind, abandoning what they had obtained, wished to go to the great giving and fell into a deep pit, so too my disciples, abandoning coarse clothing and food and chasing after the great giving to seek fine offerings, on account of worldly profit lose great wisdom and fall into the deep pit of the Avīci hell.]

Śāriputra, the born-blind who were deceived are those bhikṣus who abandon the Buddha’s unsurpassed path and pursue the outsiders’ scriptures. The swindler is the evil Māra; the deep pit is the wrong path. Śāriputra, just as the flock of the blind abandoned what they had obtained, vainly seeking to gain the great giving and so fell into a deep pit, so too my disciples, abandoning coarse clothing and food and pursuing the great giving to seek fine offerings, on account of worldly fame and profit lose great wisdom and fall into the deep pit of the Avīci hell.
[Born blind] One who is blind from birth.

[Moreover, Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma does not know the Tathāgata’s adaptive and expedient intention, and not understanding it well himself, preaches for others. Such a person obtains five faults in this present life. Other people do not know them; only the bhikṣu who has obtained the divine eye and the gods know them. What are the five? First, when preaching the Dharma he is full of fear in his heart, afraid someone may challenge him. Second, inwardly distressed and fearful, he yet preaches for others. Third, he is an ordinary person without true wisdom. Fourth, what he preaches is impure, empty of anything but words. Fifth, his speech is without order, patching together extracts everywhere. For this reason, in the assembly, his heart is filled with terror.]

Moreover, Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma does not know the Tathāgata’s adaptive intention, and not understanding it well himself, preaches rashly for others. Such a person obtains five faults in this present life. Other people do not know them; only the bhikṣu who has obtained the divine eye and the gods in heaven know them. What are the five faults? First, when preaching the Dharma he is full of fear in his heart, afraid someone may censure and refute him. Second, inwardly distressed and fearful, yet he preaches for others (not himself understanding the Buddha Dharma, yet wishing to proclaim it, so his heart is fearful). Third, he is an ordinary person without true wisdom. Fourth, what he preaches is impure — what he preaches is not the truth — but he expends his effort on fine, flowery words. Fifth, his speech is without order, rambling here and there (because he has not himself thoroughly comprehended it). For this reason, in the assembly, his heart is filled with terror.

[Not knowing the Tathāgata’s adaptive intention] The World-Honored One, in accord with the capacities of beings, spoke of the Two Vehicles and the Three Vehicles; these are expedient teachings, while the true teaching is the One Buddha Vehicle. The Lotus Sutra

Skillful Means chapter says: “In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the One Vehicle Dharma, with no second and no third, apart from the Buddha’s expedient preaching.” It also says: “Only this one thing is real; the other two are not true.” [Expedient and real] The teaching suitable for a time is called “expedient”; the ultimate and unchanging teaching is called “real.” [No second and no third, apart from the Buddha’s expedient preaching] There is no Two Vehicles and no Three Vehicles; the Two Vehicles and Three Vehicles are the Buddha’s expedient preaching. [Two Vehicles] The Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle. [Three Vehicles] The Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle. The Śrāvaka vehicle is also called the lesser vehicle; the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is also called the middle vehicle; the Bodhisattva vehicle is also called the great vehicle.

[Such an ordinary person has no wisdom and no settled mind, but from the trivial causes of pride and the like seeks fame; with doubt and regret in his heart, he preaches for others. Such a person, in the long night, himself receives the poisoned arrows of greed, hatred, and delusion. Why? Śāriputra, this person cannot definitively know the dharmas, and preaches them for others; his mind is not joyful, and if he has any joy it is quickly lost. Śāriputra, I know that impure preaching has this fault, and that it does not attain the right path. This matter all the bhikṣus do not know, the gods do not know; I alone know it.]

Such an ordinary person has no wisdom, and in his mind has no settled faith and understanding, but from the trivial causes of pride, the pursuit of profit, and the like, seeks fame; with doubt and regret in his heart, he preaches the Dharma for others. These people, in the long night, themselves receive the poisoned arrows of greed, hatred, and delusion. Why? Śāriputra, these people cannot definitively know the dharmas, and yet preach them for others; while preaching, their own minds are not joyful, and even if they have a little joy it is quickly lost. Śāriputra, I know that impure preaching has this fault, and that it does not attain the right path. This matter all the bhikṣus do not know, the gods do not know; I alone know it.

[There is also impure preaching. A bhikṣu does not understand the Tathāgata’s adaptive preaching, and preaches for others. The scriptures speak of no self, no person, no sentient being, no life; but this person, with his own arguments, says: there is a self, there is a person, there is a sentient being, there is a life. This is slandering the Buddha, slandering the Dharma, and slandering the Saṅgha. The offense of slandering the Three Jewels the gods and people of the world cannot know; only the Buddha knows it. Śāriputra, this person is also called one who impurely preaches the Dharma. I know his fault; those with supernormal powers and the multitudes of gods all cannot know it; only the Buddha knows it.]

There is also impure preaching. A bhikṣu does not understand what the Tathāgata taught in accord with the capacities of beings, and relying on his own intention preaches rashly for others. The scriptures speak of no self, no person, no sentient being, no life; but this person, with his own arguments, says: there is a self, there is a person, there is a sentient being, there is a life. This is slandering the Buddha, slandering the Dharma, and slandering the Saṅgha. The terror of this offense of slandering the Three Jewels the gods and the people of the world cannot know; only the Buddha knows it. Śāriputra, this person is also called one who impurely preaches the Dharma. I know his fault; those with supernormal powers and the multitudes of gods all cannot know it; only the Buddha knows it.
[No self, no person, no sentient being, no life] Self, others, sentient beings, and life are all illusions and do not exist at all.

[Śāriputra, I will now explain to you by a parable. If a person who does not know the meaning and characteristics of the Buddha path impurely preaches the Dharma for others, how many unwholesome matters does this person accomplish? Śāriputra, what do you think — are the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa numerous or not? “Very numerous, World-Honored One.” Śāriputra, if an evil person took away the lives of them all, would the offense of this person be great? “Very great, World-Honored One.” Just so, this deluded person who does not know the Buddha path and impurely preaches the Dharma for others incurs a greater offense than this.]

Śāriputra, I will now explain by a parable the terror of the offense of impure preaching and slandering the Three Jewels: if a person who does not know the meaning and characteristics of the Buddha path impurely preaches the Dharma for others, this person accomplishes this dangerous and evil matter. Śāriputra, what do you think — are the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa not very numerous? Śāriputra replied: “Very numerous, World-Honored One.” The World-Honored One said: “Śāriputra, if an evil person killed all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, would the offense this person obtains not be very great?” Śāriputra replied: “Very great, World-Honored One.” The World-Honored One said: “Just so, such a deluded person who does not know the Buddha path and impurely preaches the Dharma for others incurs a greater offense than this.”

[How many unwholesome matters does this person accomplish] Here “how many” has the meaning of “dangerous.” The Mozi says: “What is not firm in its root will surely be endangered at its tip.” [Jambudvīpa] Also called the southern continent; in Chinese it is translated “the Victorious Gold Continent” — that is, the Sahā world in which we dwell, also called the southern Jambudvīpa.

[Why? Because this person, impurely preaching the Dharma, destroys the unsurpassed Buddha path and also slanders the past, future, and present Buddhas. Why? Śāriputra, if there are past Buddhas, they all say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, the future Buddhas also say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, the Buddhas now present in the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, this is called the unsurpassed Dharma of the Buddhas: that all dharmas have no essence, the emptiness of non-attainment, their nature still and extinct, without arising and without ceasing, without nature and mark, their own marks all empty.]

Why? Because such a deluded person, impurely preaching the Dharma, destroys the unsurpassed Buddha path and also slanders the past, future, and present Buddhas. Why? Śāriputra, the past Buddhas all say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, the future Buddhas also all say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, the Buddhas now present in the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, also all say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, the unsurpassed Dharma of the Buddhas is this: that all dharmas have no essence, the emptiness of non-attainment, their nature still and extinct, without arising and without ceasing, without nature and mark, their own marks all empty.

[The Tathāgata speaks only for the sake of cutting off all recollections and discriminations; the Buddhas’ bodhi is without discrimination. Śāriputra, what is discrimination? What is called discrimination is the view of self, the view of person, the view of sentient being, the view of a life, the view of a soul, the annihilationist view, and the eternalist view; ordinary beings accomplish these discriminations. If a person has no such discriminations, and can fully know that all dharmas are empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul, then when he thinks thus his mind rejoices, and hearing the foremost meaning emptiness he is not startled and not afraid. This person then knows the five aggregates are false and illusory, without reality; knows the twelve sense-entrances and the eighteen elements are false and illusory, without reality. This person also does not discriminate nirvāṇa, does not think of nirvāṇa, does not say “I can think of nirvāṇa and, through the Dharma, attain stillness”; he does not discriminate. As to where the Dharma is still and extinct, he does not discriminate, nor does he obtain it. Śāriputra, this is called compliance-endurance. This person, in this compliance-endurance within the foremost meaning, also does not obtain a self-mark.]

The Tathāgata speaks only for the sake of sentient beings, to cut off all recollections and discriminations; the Buddhas’ anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is without discrimination. Śāriputra, what is discrimination? What is called discrimination is the view of self, the view of person, the view of sentient being, the view of a life, the view of a soul, the annihilationist view, and the eternalist view; ordinary beings accomplish these discriminations. If a person has no such discriminations, he can fully know that all dharmas are empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. When he thinks thus his mind rejoices; hearing the foremost meaning emptiness he is not startled and not afraid. This person then knows the five aggregates are false and illusory, without reality; knows the twelve sense-entrances and the eighteen elements are false and illusory, without reality. This person also does not discriminate nirvāṇa, does not think of nirvāṇa, and does not say “I can think of nirvāṇa and, through the Dharma, attain stillness”; he does not discriminate. As to where the Dharma is still and extinct, he does not discriminate, nor does he obtain it. Śāriputra, this is called compliance-endurance. This person, in this compliance-endurance within the foremost meaning, also does not obtain a self-mark.

[Annihilationist view] The deluded clinging that after death the five aggregates, body and mind, all cease. [Eternalist view] The deluded clinging that this five-aggregate body and mind, though they cease in this life, are reborn in a future life, continuing without interruption, abiding forever without extinction.

[The five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. These five, being accumulated and arising, are called the “five aggregates”; and because they can cover over a person’s true nature, causing him to be deluded and inverted and to create various karmas, they are also called the “five shadows.” Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called the “dharma of form”; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness belong to the mind and are called the “dharmas of mind.” These are the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Among them, the aggregate of form is the body; the other four aggregates (feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness) are the mind.

The Sutra of Complete Enlightenment says: “What is ignorance? Good man! All sentient beings, from time without beginning, have many kinds of inversion, just like a deluded person who takes the four directions to have changed places: they mistakenly take the four great elements as the form of the self, and the shadow-traces of the six sense-objects as the form of the mind. It is like one who has diseased eyes seeing flowers in the empty sky and a second moon. Good man! The sky truly has no flowers; the sick one deludedly clings to them. Because of this deluded clinging, not only is he confused about the nature of this empty sky, he is also confused about the place where the real flowers arise. From this illusion there is false existence, and he revolves in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.”

[Śāriputra, what is the mark of compliance-endurance? That which is called signlessness is the mark of compliance-endurance. Śāriputra, what do you think — if a person in this compliance-endurance does not even obtain a mark, then if this person obtained the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, the mark of a life, or the mark of a soul, that would be impossible. If a person accomplishes such wisdom, he should receive offerings; he is called a son of the Buddha, called entering the concentration of non-abiding. Śāriputra, this is called the foremost meaning gate of the Buddha Dharma, meaning without recollection and discrimination, without this and without that. But this deluded person, in the great assembly preaching wrong views, teaching others with his own recollections and discriminations — “this is the Buddha Dharma, this is the holy path” — such a deluded person slanders the past, future, and present Buddhas. Such a deluded person is called an evil spiritual friend, not a good spiritual friend.]

Śāriputra, what is the mark of compliance-endurance? That which is called signlessness is the mark of compliance-endurance. Śāriputra, what do you think — if a person in this compliance-endurance does not even obtain a mark, then if this person obtained the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, the mark of a life, or the mark of a soul, that would be impossible. If a person accomplishes such wisdom, he should receive offerings; he is called a son of the Buddha, called entering the concentration of non-abiding. Śāriputra, this is called the foremost meaning gate of the Buddha Dharma, meaning without recollection and discrimination, without this and without that. But those deluded persons, in the great assembly preaching wrong views and teaching others with their own recollections and discriminations, saying “this is the Buddha Dharma, this is the holy path” — such deluded persons slander the past, future, and present Buddhas. Such deluded persons are called evil spiritual friends, not good spiritual friends.

[Śāriputra, an enemy, though he takes life, only causes the loss of one body. But such a deluded person, impurely preaching the Dharma, in thousands of millions of eons causes great decay and affliction to sentient beings. This person’s dark delusion covers the original mind of the Buddhas’ bodhi; his greed and clinging blaze up again and again, continuing without interruption. Because of greed and clinging, he goes back and forth among the five realms, with no good path, birth and death without end. Therefore, Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma incurs very great offenses, and also serves as an evil spiritual friend to sentient beings, and also slanders the past, future, and present Buddhas.]

Śāriputra, a thieving enemy who takes life only causes the loss of one body. But such a deluded person, impurely preaching the Dharma, in thousands of millions of eons causes great decay and affliction to sentient beings. The darkness of this person’s delusion covers the Buddha-nature (the original mind of bodhi); his greed and clinging blaze up again and again, continuing without interruption. Because of greed and clinging, he goes back and forth among the five realms, and without the good path (the human and heavenly realms), birth and death have no end. Therefore, Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma incurs very great offenses, also serves as an evil spiritual friend to sentient beings, and also slanders the past, future, and present Buddhas.
[The five realms] First, the hell realm; second, the hungry ghost realm; third, the animal realm; fourth, the human realm; fifth, the heavenly realm.

[Śāriputra, not to mention the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa — if a person deprived all the sentient beings of the three-thousand great-thousand world of life, the offense of impure preaching is greater than this. Why? Because such a person destroys the Buddhas’ anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, assists the affairs of Māra, and causes sentient beings to undergo decay and affliction for hundreds of thousands of eons; he can only bind them and cannot release them. One should know that such a person is, toward sentient beings, an evil spiritual friend, one who speaks false words, and in the great assembly slanders the Buddhas; on account of these causes and conditions he falls into the great hell. He teaches many sentient beings the matter of wrong views; therefore he is called one of evil wrong views.]
Śāriputra, not to mention this taking away the lives of all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa,
if a person takes away the lives of all the sentient beings of the three-thousand great-thousand world, the offense of impure preaching is greater than this.

(Earlier it was said that the offense of impure preaching is greater than killing all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa; here it goes further, saying that the offense of impure preaching is greater than killing all the sentient beings of the three-thousand great-thousand world — a parable showing how terrifying impure preaching is!) Why does impure preaching carry such a heavy offense? Because these impure preachers all destroy the Buddhas’ anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and assist the affairs of Māra; they also cause sentient beings to undergo decay and affliction for hundreds of thousands of eons. They can only bind and cannot release. One should know that such persons are, toward sentient beings, evil spiritual friends, speaking false words, and in the great assembly slandering the Buddhas; on account of these causes and conditions they fall into the great hell. They teach many sentient beings the matter of wrong views; therefore they are called those of evil wrong views.

[Śāriputra, those with the view of self, the view of person, and the view of sentient being mostly fall into wrong views; those who eradicate these views quickly attain the path. Why? Because these are easy to abandon. For this reason, one should know that such a person would rather cut out his own tongue with a sharp knife than impurely preach the Dharma in the assembly.]

Śāriputra, those with the view of self, the view of person, and the view of sentient being mostly fall into wrong views; whereas those who have eradicated the view of self, the view of person, and the view of sentient being all quickly attain the path. Why? Because those who have eradicated the view of self, the view of person, and the view of sentient being find them easy to abandon (leaving the marks, not clinging to marks). For this reason, one should know that such deluded persons would rather cut off their own tongues with a sharp knife than impurely preach the Dharma in the assembly.

blocks.text: The Chapter on the Past, the Seventh

inline.s: In this chapter, the World-Honored One holds up the past as a mirror for the present, explaining the great retribution of impure preaching and the long eons in which its followers fall into hell; while “if a person wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and preaches the Dharma for others, he obtains immeasurable and boundless merit, and is also able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.”
[The Buddha told Śāriputra: In the past, in a distant, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable asamkhyeya eon, at that time there was a Buddha named the Tathāgata of Great Adornment, the Worthy
(the text here omits one character — “gòng,” meaning “offerings”)

, the Fully Awakened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, knower of the world, the supreme being, the tamer of men, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.]

Śākyamuni Buddha instructed Śāriputra, saying: In the past, in a distant, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable asamkhyeya eon, at that time there was a Buddha named the Tathāgata of Great Adornment, the Worthy One, the Fully Awakened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, knower of the world, the supreme being, the tamer of men, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

[Asamkhyeya] That is, asamkhyeya; in Chinese it is translated “countless,” meaning so many that no number can count them. [The Tathāgata’s titles] The Tathāgata has the following honorific titles: First, the Tathāgata — one who, by the path of suchness, comes and attains right enlightenment. Second, the Worthy One — worthy of the offerings of humans and gods. Third, the Fully Awakened One — truly and universally knowing all dharmas. Fourth, perfect in knowledge and conduct — possessing the three insights of the insight into past lives, the divine eye, and the insight into the extinction of outflows, together with the five conducts of holy conduct, brahma conduct, heavenly conduct, infant conduct, and sick conduct, all complete. Fifth, the Well-Gone One — freely and well gone, entering nirvāṇa. Sixth, knower of the world — able to understand the principle of all worldly matters. Seventh, the supreme being — the one supreme and unrivaled. Eighth, the tamer of men — the great man who can tame and guide beings to the right path. Ninth, the teacher of gods and humans — the Buddha is the teacher of all gods and humans. Tenth, the Buddha — in Sanskrit the full title is “Buddha”; in Chinese “the Awakened One,” meaning wisdom fully complete and the three enlightenments consummated (self-enlightenment, enlightening others, and enlightenment-and-practice consummated), knowing and seeing all dharmas of the three times. Eleventh, the World-Honored One — the Buddha is the one whom all the people of the world jointly revere.

[That Buddha’s lifespan was sixty-eight hundred million nayuta years, and he had sixty-eight hundred million nayuta great disciples. After that Buddha passed into extinction, his relics were distributed everywhere, exactly as after my extinction. His right Dharma also abided in the world for five hundred years, exactly as after my extinction.]

The Tathāgata of Great Adornment’s lifespan was sixty-eight hundred million nayuta years, and he had sixty-eight hundred million nayuta great disciples. After the Tathāgata of Great Adornment passed into extinction, his relics were distributed throughout the four quarters, exactly the same as after my extinction. The right Dharma of the Tathāgata of Great Adornment also abided in the world for five hundred years, exactly the same as after my extinction.

[After that Buddha passed into extinction, among his great disciples, in one day there were a hundred bhikṣus who entered nirvāṇa; two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, five hundred entered nirvāṇa; in one day there might even be a hundred thousand nayuta bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa. Thus in turn, all of that Buddha’s greatly wise, greatly learned, and greatly supernaturally powerful assembly entered nirvāṇa within three months.]

After the Tathāgata of Great Adornment passed into extinction, among his great disciples, in one day there were a hundred bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa; in one day there were two hundred bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa; in one day there were three hundred bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa; in one day there were four hundred bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa; in one day there were five hundred bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa; and even in one day there might be a hundred thousand nayuta bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa. Thus in turn, all of that Buddha’s greatly wise, greatly learned, and greatly supernaturally powerful assembly entered nirvāṇa one after another within three months.
[All successively entered nirvāṇa] Because the great disciples had all realized the fruit of arhat, coming and going freely, they themselves could decide when to enter nirvāṇa.

[Śāriputra, the right Dharma of the Buddha of Great Adornment spread abroad, and many gods and people together made offerings to it. Śāriputra, after the Buddha of Great Adornment and his great disciples passed into extinction, gradually many people came to know that the Dharma of the śramaṇas is secure and joyful, and left home to study the path, but they could not understand the unequaled meaning of emptiness of the profound sutras preached by the Buddha, and were mostly deluded by the evil Māra. At that time, the preachers’ minds were not settled, and their preaching was impure; they spoke of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life, and did not speak of all dharmas as empty and still.]

Śāriputra, the right Dharma of the Buddha of Great Adornment spread abroad, and very many hosts of gods and people together made offerings to it. Śāriputra, after the Buddha of Great Adornment and his great disciples passed into extinction, gradually many people came to know that the Dharma of the śramaṇas is secure and happy, and so left home to study the path; yet they could not understand the unequaled meaning of emptiness of the profound sutras spoken by the Buddha (because the great disciples of the Tathāgata of Great Adornment had all entered nirvāṇa), and were mostly deluded by the evil Māra. At that time, the preachers had no settled faith in the Buddha’s right Dharma (no unshakable, single-minded faith free of doubt); most preached impurely, deludedly clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life as really existing, and did not speak of all dharmas as empty and still.
[Secure (anyin)] That is, “secure and at ease.”

[Having a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life] This is what the Diamond Sutra calls the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, and the mark of a life. The Buddha said: “If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, and the mark of a life, he is not a bodhisattva.” [The mark of self] Deludedly clinging to the five-aggregate body and mind as real, and taking it as “self” and giving rise to the mind — for example, gain and loss, favorable and adverse, honor and disgrace, and so on. [The mark of person] Deludedly clinging to the other party, to other people, as really existing and giving rise to the mind — for example, love and hate, right and wrong, high and low, and so on. [The mark of sentient being] Here “sentient beings” refers to groups of people, for example groups distinguished by closeness and distance, likes and dislikes, friend and enemy, age, sex, work unit, region, ethnicity, skin color, country, and so on. The mark of sentient being is deludedly clinging to these groups of people as real and giving rise to a discriminative mind. [The mark of a life] Deludedly clinging to a life-span as real and reckoning its length or shortness. Of all the things the deluded sentient beings care about most, there is nothing more than a life-span; therefore the mark of a life is separated out from the mark of self and set up as its own item.
